title: AI Unlocked: The Humanities
blurb: For writers, historians, linguists, artists, and scholars: research and archival workflows, translation and close-reading at scale, creative collaboration without losing your voice, and the authorship debates every humanist must be able to argue.

modules.d: Why AI is a humanities question as much as a technical one — and what humanists uniquely bring.
modules.body:
AI is built from human culture

Large language models are trained on vast quantities of human writing: books, articles, websites, translations, conversations. Image models learn from human art and photography. In a real sense, generative AI is a compression of human culture — and the humanities, which study that culture, language, meaning and value, are directly implicated. Questions about what these systems "understand", whose voices they represent, what they omit and how they change creativity are humanities questions.

What do language models do?

Language models predict likely sequences of text based on patterns learned from training data. Researchers debate how to describe their capabilities. Emily Bender, Timnit Gebru and colleagues famously described large language models as "stochastic parrots" — producing fluent language without grounded understanding — and warned about bias, environmental cost and the illusion of meaning. Others argue the systems develop useful internal representations. Humanists need not settle this debate to use AI wisely, but they should resist both hype ("it understands everything") and dismissal ("it is just autocomplete"), and judge outputs critically.

Fluency is not truth. Language models can produce elegant prose, confident interpretation and plausible citations that are entirely fabricated. Humanist training — close reading, source criticism, contextual knowledge — is exactly what is needed to detect when fluent text is wrong.

Whose culture? Representation and bias

Training data over-represents widely published languages, cultures and perspectives — especially English and the Global North — and under-represents many African, Indigenous and minority languages and oral traditions. AI outputs can therefore reproduce stereotypes, flatten cultural nuance, or present one tradition's assumptions as universal. Humanists can identify these distortions, contribute better data and descriptions, and advocate for inclusion — for instance through community initiatives building language technology for African languages.

What humanists bring

  • Interpretation: meaning depends on context, genre, history and audience — not just words.
  • Source criticism: evaluating provenance, reliability and bias of evidence.
  • Ethical reasoning: questions of authorship, dignity, representation and responsibility.
  • Language expertise: translation, rhetoric, multilingual nuance.
  • Historical perspective: earlier technologies — printing, photography, the internet — also transformed authorship and knowledge, offering lessons for today.
  • Creativity and voice: the distinctive perspective that makes work worth reading.

Opportunities

AI can accelerate transcription of archives, translation drafts, analysis of large text collections, discovery of patterns across centuries of documents, and creative experimentation. Used critically, it extends the reach of humanistic inquiry. Used uncritically, it produces superficial scholarship and homogenised art.

The stance of this course

We approach AI as humanists: curious, critical, historically informed and ethically serious. The goal is not to defend the humanities against AI, nor to surrender them to it, but to bring humanistic judgement to how AI is used — in research, teaching, translation and art.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my critical discussion partner. I am a [writer/historian/linguist/artist/scholar]. Help me map where AI could help my work and where it could distort it, citing specific risks such as fabrication, cultural bias and loss of voice. Then pose three challenging questions about authorship, representation and meaning that my discipline is particularly well placed to answer.

📚 Glossary

  • Language model: AI system predicting text from learned patterns
  • Stochastic parrots: critique describing LLMs as fluent without grounded understanding
  • Source criticism: evaluating the origin and reliability of evidence
  • Representation bias: over- or under-representation of groups in data and outputs

📖 References

  • Bender, E., Gebru, T. et al. (2021). On the dangers of stochastic parrots: can language models be too big? FAccT.
  • Crawford, K. (2021). Atlas of AI.
  • Masakhane — participatory research on NLP for African languages (masakhane.io).
  • Eisenstein, E. (1979). The Printing Press as an Agent of Change.

quiz.q: A literature student in Buea submits an AI-generated essay on Achebe's Things Fall Apart, arguing it must be accurate because the prose is polished and confident. As her tutor, what is the best response?
opts: Accept the argument but lower the mark because she did not write it herself
Ask her to rerun the essay through a second chatbot to confirm its conclusions
Have her check each claim and quote against the novel and reliable criticism
Agree the style is strong, then ask her to add the page references the AI can supply
quiz.x: Fluency is not truth: claims must be checked against the text and sources. A second chatbot (runner-up) may repeat the same fabrications, and AI-supplied page numbers are a classic fabrication risk.

quiz.q: At a Yaounde faculty seminar, one colleague says LLMs understand literature as people do; another says they are mere autocomplete. Which position best matches the stance this module recommends?
opts: Ban AI from the seminar until researchers agree on what the models understand
Side with the capability camp, since internal representations show real comprehension
Side with the dismissal camp, since the stochastic parrots paper settled the question
Avoid both hype and dismissal, and judge each output critically on its merits
quiz.x: The module says humanists need not settle the debate but should resist both hype and dismissal and judge outputs critically. Treating the parrots paper as settling it overstates a contested argument.

quiz.q: An AI summary of a Bamileke oral tradition presents it using categories from Greek mythology, calling a founding ancestor a 'Zeus figure'. What is the most accurate diagnosis of the problem?
opts: A hallucination that a better prompt asking for accuracy would reliably fix
Representation bias: one tradition's assumptions presented as universal
A copyright issue, because oral traditions belong to the community that holds them
A translation slip caused by the model working in English instead of French
quiz.x: Training data over-represents Global North traditions, so outputs flatten nuance by imposing their frames. Calling it a mere hallucination fixed by prompting misses the structural bias in the data.

quiz.q: A history lecturer receives an AI-written report citing a 1962 article in a journal that sounds right but that she has never seen. Which humanist skill helps her most in deciding what to do next?
opts: Source criticism: checking the cited work's existence, origin and reliability
Historical perspective: comparing this with errors in early printed books
Ethical reasoning: weighing whether the student meant to deceive her
Close reading: analysing the report's rhetoric for signs of machine phrasing
quiz.x: Source criticism tests whether evidence exists and is reliable, which is exactly what a possibly fabricated citation needs. Close reading for machine phrasing is a runner-up but cannot confirm whether the article exists.

quiz.q: A panel debating AI in Douala asks why a historian's view of printing, photography and the internet is useful today. Which answer best reflects the module's argument?
opts: It shows that regulation tends to arrive too late to shape a new technology
It lets historians predict the exact jobs AI will remove in the next decade
It shows how earlier technologies reshaped authorship, authority and error, offering lessons
It shows each new technology was eventually harmless, so present worries are overblown
quiz.x: The module says earlier technologies such as print transformed authorship and knowledge, offering lessons. Concluding that they were harmless (runner-up) is a misreading that ignores the real disruption they caused.

quiz.q: A US museum director plans an AI strategy for her humanities staff. Which framing best captures the stance the course takes toward AI?
opts: Bring humanistic judgement to how AI is used in research, teaching and art
Wait for AI vendors to publish ethics guidance before taking any position
Adopt AI widely, since tools now handle interpretation better than most staff
Protect the humanities by keeping AI out of research and teaching wherever possible
quiz.x: The course aims neither to defend the humanities against AI nor to surrender to it, but to apply humanistic judgement to its use. Keeping AI out (runner-up) is the defensive stance the course explicitly rejects.

quiz.q: A linguist notes that a chatbot handles French well but produces poor Ghomala' and Bulu text. Cameroon has about 250 languages. What best explains the gap?
opts: Their speakers have refused to allow their languages to be used for training
Little text in these languages exists online, so training data is thin
Developers filter African languages out to reduce computing costs
These languages are grammatically too complex for current model architectures
quiz.x: Training data over-represents widely published languages; most of Cameroon's languages are barely present online. Claiming grammatical complexity is a common misconception: the limit is data, not inherent difficulty.

quiz.q: A research team in Nairobi has 30 years of digitised parliamentary debates. Which AI use best extends humanistic inquiry rather than replacing it?
opts: Generating summaries of each session to replace reading the original transcripts
Using AI to rank which speakers were the most persuasive in each debate
Asking a chatbot to write the team's final interpretive article from the debates
Tracing vocabulary across decades, then interpreting it by reading closely
quiz.x: Pattern discovery across large collections, followed by human interpretation, extends inquiry. Persuasiveness ranking (runner-up) outsources an interpretive judgement that depends on context the model cannot weigh.

quiz.q: An AI tool reads a Nigerian Pidgin poem's line 'Wahala no dey finish' purely as literal complaint, missing its ironic, communal tone. What does 'interpretation depends on context' imply here?
opts: The poem should be translated into standard English before any analysis is done
Meaning depends on genre, history and audience, so the AI reading needs critique
AI readings are acceptable if the model's output cites the line correctly
The ironic reading is just one opinion, so the AI's literal reading is equally valid
quiz.x: Meaning depends on context, genre, history and audience, not just words; humanists should critique such readings. Treating all readings as equal (runner-up) ignores that some readings are better supported by context.

quiz.q: A dean in Johannesburg asks why humanities departments, not just computer science, should help shape policy on generative AI. Which reason best reflects the module?
opts: Humanities departments are better funded for AI research than engineering ones
Computer scientists lack the technical skill to evaluate language model outputs
AI is built from human writing and art, raising questions of meaning and voice
Generative AI mostly produces creative work, which falls under the arts by default
quiz.x: Generative AI is in a sense a compression of human culture, so questions of understanding, voice and omission are humanities questions. Saying AI mostly produces art (runner-up) is narrower and misses the cultural-data point.

facts.t: Year Bender, Gebru and colleagues published 'On the Dangers of Stochastic Parrots'.
facts.more: The paper warned that fluent language is not grounded understanding, and flagged bias, environmental cost and the illusion of meaning.

facts.t: Living languages spoken in the world today.
facts.more: Only a small fraction are well represented online, so AI training data over-represents English and the Global North.

facts.t: Approximate number of languages spoken in Cameroon.
facts.more: One of Africa's most linguistically diverse countries — and most of these languages are barely present in AI training data.

facts.t: Gutenberg's movable-type press transforms European book production.
facts.more: Printing also reshaped authorship, authority and error. Earlier technologies offer humanists lessons for today's AI shift.

labs.title: Hype, dismissal, or critical judgement?
labs.intro: Sort these statements about language models.
items: It understands literature better than any critic
Its interpretations are final — no need to read the novel
It's just autocomplete; nothing useful can come of it
Humanists should ignore it entirely
Fluent output must still be checked against sources
It may reflect Global North assumptions; test it on local texts
Useful for drafts; meaning still depends on context and audience
labs.tip: Resist both 'it understands everything' and 'it's just autocomplete' — judge the output.

labs.title: Read this AI answer critically
labs.intro: Asked about Bamenda's oral traditions, an AI replied. Tap what a humanist should challenge.
segments: Oral traditions in the Grassfields carry history, law and genealogy across generations.
Storytellers adapt performance to audience and occasion.
As Professor Jean Mbarga wrote in his 1987 classic 'Voices of the Hills',
Plausible but unverified author and title — likely fabricated. Locate it before citing.
these traditions are primitive precursors to written history.
Loaded, Eurocentric framing presented as neutral fact.
All Grassfields peoples share exactly the same stories and customs.
Flattens cultural diversity — a typical AI generalisation.
Recording them requires the consent of the communities concerned.
Many are now being documented by local researchers.
labs.tip: Fluency is not truth: question sources, framing and generalisations.

plaibox.title: Simulation: the museum label
plaibox.intro: You curate a small exhibition on Cameroonian masks in Yaoundé and use AI to draft labels.
plaibox.win: Fine humanist judgement: you checked sources, respected communities and kept interpretation human.
plaibox.lose: Revisit the module: fluency is not truth, and whose culture matters.

steps.s: The AI's label describes a mask's 'meaning' confidently, citing no source.
o: Publish it; it reads beautifully and visitors will love it
Fluent text can be invented; the label would spread error.
Check it against provenance records and specialist literature
Source criticism is exactly the humanist's job.
Delete the meaning section entirely to avoid any risk
Cautious, but you lose context visitors need; verify instead.

steps.s: The draft calls the mask 'tribal art', a phrase community members dislike.
o: Keep it; it's common in catalogues
Common usage can carry outdated, distorting assumptions.
Consult community members on how they name the object
Representation and dignity are humanities questions; ask those concerned.
Replace it with a neutral term you choose alone
Better, but still decides for the community without them.

steps.s: A colleague says AI labels are 'just autocomplete' and should be banned.
o: Agree and stop all AI use
Safe, but dismissal ignores useful drafting help.
Use AI for drafts; humans verify and interpret
Neither hype nor dismissal — critical use.
Tell them AI understands art better than curators
Hype; it overstates what the system does.

modules.d: Transcription, discovery, note-taking and citation — with verification at the core.
modules.body:
Accelerating the research cycle

Humanities research involves finding sources, reading and annotating, transcribing and translating, organising notes, developing arguments and citing accurately. AI can accelerate several steps — but scholarship stands or falls on the accuracy of sources and citations.

Archives and transcription

Many archives contain handwritten letters, administrative records, missionary diaries, colonial reports and community documents that are hard to read and impossible to search. Handwritten text recognition (HTR) platforms such as Transkribus can be trained on samples of a particular hand or script and then transcribe large collections, making them searchable. Optical character recognition (OCR) does the same for printed text. Accuracy varies with script, language and document condition, so transcriptions require sampling and correction before scholarly use.

The fabricated citation problem. General AI chatbots frequently invent references — plausible authors, titles, journals and page numbers that do not exist. A 2023 study in Scientific Reports found that a majority of citations produced by one widely used chatbot model, and a smaller but significant share from a newer model, were fabricated. Never cite a source you have not located and checked yourself.

Discovery and literature review

AI research assistants can suggest search terms, summarise abstracts, map debates and identify gaps. Use them to orient yourself, then go to library catalogues, scholarly databases and the texts themselves. Be aware that AI tools often reflect the most-cited, English-language scholarship and may miss regional journals, African publications and non-digitised sources — exactly where original contributions often lie.

Reading, annotation and notes

AI can summarise long texts, but summaries lose nuance, argumentative structure and the details that matter for interpretation. Use summaries to decide what to read closely, not as substitutes for reading. Reference managers such as Zotero store sources and notes and generate bibliographies in standard styles; keep verified bibliographic data there rather than relying on AI-generated references.

Working with sensitive materials

Archives may contain personal information about living people, sacred or restricted cultural knowledge, or materials governed by copyright or institutional rules. Before uploading documents to AI tools, check archive terms, privacy and copyright, and the wishes of communities connected to the materials. Some knowledge is not meant for public circulation.

Oral history

Speech-to-text tools can transcribe interviews quickly, but quality varies by language, accent and recording conditions, and transcription is itself interpretive — choices about punctuation, dialect and silence shape meaning. Obtain informed consent for recording, transcription and any use of AI tools; return transcripts to interviewees where appropriate; and follow oral history ethics.

A verified research workflow

  1. Use AI to brainstorm questions and search terms.
  2. Find sources through catalogues, databases and archives.
  3. Verify every source exists and says what you think it says.
  4. Use AI to transcribe, translate drafts or summarise — then check.
  5. Write your argument in your own words, with your own interpretation.
  6. Cite from your reference manager, and disclose AI use as required by your institution or publisher.
🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my research assistant for a humanities project on [topic]. Suggest 15 search terms in English and French, key debates I should explore, and types of archives and databases to consult, including African and regional sources. Do NOT invent citations — instead tell me what kinds of sources to look for. Then design a verification checklist for any transcription or translation I produce with AI.

📚 Glossary

  • HTR: handwritten text recognition
  • OCR: optical character recognition for printed text
  • Transkribus: platform for transcribing historical documents with HTR
  • Reference manager: software storing sources and generating citations, e.g., Zotero
  • Oral history: recorded interviews preserving personal and community memory

📖 References

  • Walters, W. & Wilder, E. (2023). Fabrication and errors in the bibliographic citations generated by ChatGPT. Scientific Reports.
  • READ-COOP — Transkribus documentation.
  • Oral History Association — Principles and Best Practices.
  • Zotero documentation (zotero.org).

quiz.q: A master's student in Yaounde asks a chatbot for sources and gets five articles supporting her thesis, each with authors, journal and page numbers. What should she do before citing any of them?
opts: Cite them but add a note that the references were found with AI assistance
Ask the chatbot to confirm each reference is real and give its DOI number
Keep the three that look most plausible and replace the other two later
Find each one in a catalogue or database and confirm it says what is claimed
quiz.x: Walters and Wilder found many chatbot citations were fabricated, so each must be located and checked. Asking the chatbot to confirm (runner-up) feels careful but it can fabricate DOIs and confirmations too.

quiz.q: A historian has 4,000 handwritten colonial administrative letters from Bamenda in a single clerk's hand. What is the most efficient sound approach to making them searchable?
opts: Train an HTR model on samples of the hand, then sample and correct its output
Hire assistants to transcribe every letter by hand before any AI is involved
Upload the scans to a general chatbot and ask it to transcribe each one
Run printed-text OCR on the scans and correct errors as they appear in research
quiz.x: HTR platforms such as Transkribus can be trained on one hand, then outputs are sampled and corrected. OCR (runner-up) is designed for printed text and will perform poorly on handwriting.

quiz.q: A Ghanaian historian's AI literature review on colonial cocoa trade lists only British and American books. Why might the tool have missed important regional scholarship?
opts: Regional journals are generally peer-reviewed less strictly, so tools filter them out
The historian's prompt was too short for the model to search properly
AI tools favour highly cited, English-language, digitised work over local sources
African scholarship on this topic was mostly published after the model's cutoff
quiz.x: AI tools often reflect the most-cited English-language scholarship and miss regional, African and non-digitised sources. Blaming the prompt (runner-up) misses the structural bias in what the tools have seen.

quiz.q: Pressed for time, a PhD candidate in Atlanta uses an AI summary of a 300-page missionary diary instead of reading it, then quotes the summary's claims in his chapter. What is the main risk?
opts: The summary may breach the archive's copyright by reproducing the diary's text
Readers may notice his writing style differs from the summary's phrasing
The examiners may object that he used AI without logging it in a reference manager
The summary drops nuance and detail needed for interpretation, and may misstate it
quiz.x: Summaries lose nuance and argumentative detail; use them to decide what to read closely, not as substitutes. Copyright (runner-up) is a real concern for uploads, but the core scholarly risk is misrepresenting the source.

quiz.q: A researcher wants to upload a community archive from the Grassfields that includes sacred knowledge to an online AI tool for analysis. What should come first?
opts: Check archive terms, privacy, copyright and the wishes of the connected community
Upload a small test batch first to see whether the tool handles the script well
Remove names from the files, then upload since anonymised data raises no concerns
Get approval from the university IT department for the tool's security settings
quiz.x: Before uploading, check archive terms, privacy, copyright and community wishes; some knowledge is not meant for public circulation. Anonymising (runner-up) helps privacy but does not address restricted cultural knowledge.

quiz.q: An oral historian in Kumba notices that the AI transcript of an interview removed long pauses and standardised Pidgin into English. Why does the module call transcription interpretive?
opts: Because transcripts are legally the interviewer's work rather than the speaker's
Choices about punctuation, dialect and silence shape how the speaker's meaning is read
Because transcription software uses statistics, so outputs vary from one run to another
Because accents make speech-to-text output too unreliable for scholarly use
quiz.x: Transcription choices about punctuation, dialect and silence shape meaning. Calling the output unreliable (runner-up) is about accuracy, not the interpretive nature of every transcription choice.

quiz.q: A doctoral student in Lagos has 600 sources, some found via AI suggestions and since checked in the library. Where should the verified bibliographic data live for the thesis?
opts: In a reference manager such as Zotero, which generates formatted bibliographies
In a spreadsheet that the AI tool reformats into the required citation style
In the draft itself, where each reference can be retyped as the chapter evolves
In the chat history, so the AI can regenerate formatted references on request
quiz.x: The module advises keeping verified data in a reference manager such as Zotero rather than relying on AI-generated references. A spreadsheet reformatted by AI (runner-up) reintroduces the risk of altered details.

quiz.q: In Walters and Wilder's 2023 test, about 55% of GPT-3.5 and 18% of GPT-4 citations were fabricated. If a newer-model draft contains 50 references, roughly how many might be fake at that rate?
opts: About 5, so spot-checking a few references is enough
About 28, so the draft should be discarded and rewritten
About 18, so roughly a third would need replacing
About 9, so every reference still needs to be checked
quiz.x: 18% of 50 is 9. Even at the lower rate, every reference must be located and checked. The 18 figure confuses the percentage with a count; spot-checking leaves fabrications in place.

quiz.q: A community project in Limbe records elders' memories and plans to run the recordings through a cloud speech-to-text tool. Which ethical step matters most?
opts: Publishing the transcripts openly so the community can benefit quickly
Choosing the speech-to-text tool with the lowest published error rate
Informed consent covering recording, transcription and use of AI tools
Asking a relative to sign the consent form for elders who are slow to respond
quiz.x: Oral history ethics require informed consent for recording, transcription and AI use, and returning transcripts where appropriate. Picking the most accurate tool (runner-up) improves quality but does not address consent.

quiz.q: A researcher has used AI to brainstorm search terms and has found sources in catalogues and archives. According to the verified workflow, what is the next step?
opts: Write the argument in her own words using notes from the sources
Verify that every source exists and says what she thinks it says
Use AI to transcribe and summarise the sources so drafting can begin
Cite the sources from her reference manager and disclose AI use
quiz.x: The workflow runs: brainstorm, find sources, verify each source, then use AI for transcription or summaries, then write and cite. Jumping to AI transcription (runner-up) skips verification.

facts.t: Share of fabricated citations from GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 in one 2023 test.
facts.more: Walters and Wilder asked the chatbots for literature reviews and checked every reference. Never cite a source you have not located yourself.

facts.t: Handwritten text recognition — trainable on one hand or script.
facts.more: Platforms such as Transkribus learn a particular hand from samples, then transcribe whole collections. Accuracy varies: sample and correct before scholarly use.

facts.t: Optical character recognition: the printed-text counterpart of HTR.
facts.more: Old typefaces, faded ink and mixed languages raise error rates — always check a sample against the page.

facts.t: Free, open-source reference manager for verified sources and notes.
facts.more: Store checked bibliographic data there rather than trusting AI-generated references.

labs.intro: Order a responsible AI-assisted archival workflow.
steps: Check archive terms, privacy and community wishes

labs.title: Audit this AI literature review
labs.intro: An AI drafted part of a review on colonial education in Cameroon. Tap the problems.
segments: Mission schools played a major role in early formal education in both the British and French territories.
Language policy differed between the two administrations.
A 2019 article by Fonkeng and Smith in the Journal of African Schooling, vol. 12, pp. 44–61,
Specific-looking reference that may not exist — locate it in a catalogue first.
proves that all mission schools taught only in English.
Overclaims ('proves', 'all') and is implausible for French-administered areas.
Local-language and regional publications deserve attention,
but since they are not online they can safely be ignored.
Undigitised regional sources are often where original contributions lie.
Further archival work is needed.
labs.tip: Check every reference, and look beyond what is digitised and English-language.

modules.d: Machine translation, multilingual scholarship, and the difference between close and distant reading.
modules.body:
Translation is interpretation

Every translation makes choices: tone, register, cultural references, wordplay, rhythm, ambiguity. Machine translation (MT) and large language models now produce fluent drafts between many languages, transforming everyday multilingual work. For humanists, the question is not whether AI translates, but how to use it without losing what matters.

What machine translation does well — and poorly

Modern MT performs best between widely represented languages and for straightforward informational text. It struggles with literary style, irony, idioms, culturally specific concepts, archaic language, dialects, code-switching and low-resource languages — including many African languages. It may also produce smooth but wrong translations, quietly normalising unusual phrasing that carries meaning.

Domestication and foreignisation. Translation theorist Lawrence Venuti distinguished domesticating translation, which makes a text read smoothly in the target culture, from foreignising translation, which preserves the foreignness of the original. Machine translation tends to domesticate — producing fluent, familiar prose that can erase cultural difference. Humanists must decide deliberately which approach serves the text and readers.

A professional AI-assisted translation workflow

  1. Understand the source: genre, purpose, audience, cultural context.
  2. Machine draft: generate a first draft, possibly from more than one system to compare.
  3. Post-edit: revise for accuracy, register, terminology and style — line by line against the source.
  4. Check culture-specific elements: proverbs, names, forms of address, religious or legal terms.
  5. Review: ideally by a second fluent reader; for publication, by a qualified translator.
  6. Disclose: state how translation was produced where academic or publishing norms require it.

In bilingual contexts such as Cameroon — English and French, alongside many national languages and Cameroonian Pidgin English — translation is everyday civic and scholarly work. AI can speed it up, but terms with legal, religious or cultural weight need human expertise.

Close reading in an AI age

Close reading — attentive analysis of language, form, imagery and structure — remains the core of literary and textual interpretation. AI can support it: identifying rhetorical devices, tracking motifs, comparing translations, or generating counter-readings to test your interpretation. But AI interpretations are generalised; your reading must engage the specific text, its history and its critical conversation.

Distant reading and text analysis

Franco Moretti proposed distant reading: studying large numbers of texts computationally to see patterns invisible to individual reading — genre change, vocabulary shifts, networks of characters. Text analysis tools (word frequencies, topic modelling, named entity recognition) and AI can analyse whole archives or literatures. The insight comes from combining distant patterns with close interpretation: numbers raise questions that reading answers.

Language technology for African languages

Communities of researchers, including the Masakhane initiative, are building datasets and models for African languages, often participatory and community-led. Humanists — linguists, translators, writers — are essential contributors, ensuring that language technology respects grammar, culture and speakers' priorities.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my translation editor. I will paste a short source passage and a machine translation. Compare them line by line, identify errors in meaning, register, idiom and culturally specific terms, explain whether the translation domesticates or foreignises, and propose a revised translation with notes on each choice. Flag terms that need an expert or native-speaker check.

📚 Glossary

  • Machine translation: automatic translation by software
  • Post-editing: human revision of machine-translated text
  • Domestication / foreignisation: making a translation familiar versus preserving its foreignness
  • Close reading: attentive analysis of a text's language and form
  • Distant reading: computational analysis of many texts to find patterns

📖 References

  • Venuti, L. (1995). The Translator's Invisibility.
  • Moretti, F. (2013). Distant Reading.
  • Masakhane (masakhane.io) — African languages NLP research.
  • ISO 18587:2017 — Post-editing of machine translation output.

quiz.q: A machine translation renders a Bulu proverb into smooth English that reads like a familiar Western saying, losing its local imagery. In Venuti's terms, what has happened?
opts: Domestication: the text was made familiar, erasing cultural difference
Post-editing: a human reviser normalised the phrasing for readers
Foreignisation: the translation keeps the source's strangeness for the reader
Back-translation: the system translated through French and lost detail
quiz.x: MT tends to domesticate, producing familiar prose that can erase cultural difference. Foreignisation (runner-up term) would preserve the proverb's local imagery, which is the opposite of what happened.

quiz.q: A Cameroonian NGO needs four texts translated from French into English. Which is machine translation most likely to handle well with light post-editing?
opts: A nineteenth-century missionary letter in archaic French
A praise poem dense with references to local chieftaincy rites
A Pidgin-laced short story full of code-switching and wordplay
Plain instructions for registering on a health portal
quiz.x: MT performs best on straightforward informational text between well-represented languages. The archaic letter (runner-up) is in French, a well-served language, but archaic language is a known weakness.

quiz.q: A Montreal publisher hires a translator to 'post-edit' an MT draft of a novel and offers a proofreading rate. Under ISO 18587 and the module, what is post-editing?
opts: Running the text through a second MT system to correct the first
A final read by the author to approve the translator's choices
Line-by-line revision for accuracy, register, terminology and style
A quick proofread of spelling and punctuation in the machine output
quiz.x: Post-editing is professional line-by-line revision against the source; ISO 18587 treats it as a skilled task, not a quick proofread. Running a second system (runner-up) is a drafting step, not post-editing.

quiz.q: A text-analysis tool shows the word 'freedom' rises sharply in Cameroonian newspapers between 1955 and 1961. What is the best next scholarly step?
opts: Run topic modelling to confirm the trend with a second method
Read the articles closely to see how the word is used and by whom
Report the rise as evidence that public opinion turned toward independence
Compare the frequency with French newspapers from the same period
quiz.x: In distant reading, numbers raise questions that close reading answers. Topic modelling (runner-up) adds more pattern data but still cannot say what 'freedom' meant in context.

quiz.q: A Douala firm is preparing an AI-assisted translation of a land-tenure decree for public release. Which practice most improves reliability?
opts: A second fluent reader's review, with legal terms checked by an expert
Asking the AI to explain its translation choices for each sentence
Generating drafts from two MT systems and choosing the smoother version
Translating back into French to see whether the meaning survives
quiz.x: The workflow calls for review by a second fluent reader and expert checks of legal, religious or cultural terms. Back-translation (runner-up) can flag gross errors but misses register and legal nuance.

quiz.q: A Kenyan lecturer designs a course module that combines computational analysis of thousands of novels with close reading. Whose concept of studying large text collections is she drawing on?
opts: Emily Bender's idea of stochastic parrots
Franco Moretti's idea of distant reading
Lawrence Venuti's idea of foreignising translation
Roland Barthes's idea of the death of the author
quiz.x: Moretti proposed distant reading, collected in his 2013 book. Venuti (runner-up for a translation-focused course) wrote on domestication and foreignisation, not computational corpus analysis.

quiz.q: A Yaounde court interpreter uses MT to draft an English version of a French customary-law ruling. Why do terms with legal or religious weight need human expertise?
opts: MT systems are banned from use in Cameroonian court proceedings
English and French legal vocabulary is identical, so errors are rare
MT cannot process long documents such as full court rulings
Their meaning rests on context and consequence MT may flatten
quiz.x: Terms with legal, religious or cultural weight carry meaning MT can quietly normalise, with real consequences. Claiming a ban (runner-up for caution) is not stated in the module and is not the reason given.

quiz.q: A literature student in Ohio wants to use AI while writing a close reading of a Soyinka poem. Which use best supports close reading without replacing it?
opts: Ask AI to summarise critics' views so she can skip the secondary sources
Ask AI for a full interpretation, then paraphrase it into her own essay
Ask AI to propose counter-readings, then test them against the text
Ask AI to rate how persuasive her finished interpretation is
quiz.x: AI can generate counter-readings to test an interpretation, but her reading must engage the specific text. Rating persuasiveness (runner-up) gives feedback but does not deepen engagement with the poem.

quiz.q: A Cameroonian linguist wants to contribute to language technology for Ewondo. Which role best reflects how initiatives such as Masakhane work?
opts: Selling recordings to large AI companies so they add Ewondo to their models
Waiting for global models to improve enough to cover Ewondo automatically
Writing a policy paper urging the government to fund a national chatbot
Giving data and expertise so tools respect grammar and speakers' priorities
quiz.x: Masakhane-style work is community-led, with linguists and translators ensuring tools respect grammar, culture and speakers' priorities. Selling data (runner-up) may add the language but bypasses community direction.

quiz.q: A translator publishes an English edition of a Francophone Cameroonian memoir, using MT for the first draft and heavy post-editing. When should she disclose the AI involvement?
opts: Where academic or publishing norms require it, stating the method
Upon request from a reviewer who suspects machine translation
Not at all, since her post-editing made the text her own work
In the acknowledgements, but naming no specific tool or method
quiz.x: The workflow ends with disclosure where academic or publishing norms require it. Claiming post-editing removes the need to disclose (runner-up) ignores norms that expect transparency about the process.

facts.t: Venuti's 'The Translator's Invisibility' sets out domestication vs foreignisation.
facts.more: Machine translation tends to domesticate — smooth, familiar prose that can erase cultural difference.

modules.t: Creative Collaboration Without Losing Your Voice
modules.d: Using AI in writing and art as a collaborator — while protecting originality, voice and craft.
modules.body:
The creative question

Writers, poets, visual artists, musicians and filmmakers face a new kind of collaborator: a system that can generate text, images and sound instantly. Some artists refuse it; some embrace it; many experiment cautiously. The central question is not whether to use AI, but how to use it while keeping what makes your work yours — your voice, perspective, craft and integrity.

Modes of collaboration

  • Brainstorming partner: generating many possibilities you then select from, reject or transform.
  • Critic and editor: asking for feedback on clarity, pacing or structure — you decide what to change.
  • Research assistant: background on settings, periods, techniques — verified independently.
  • Constraint generator: prompts, forms or rules that push you out of habits.
  • Material: some artists work with AI outputs deliberately as raw material, exploring the technology itself as subject.
  • Production support: formatting, transcription, translation drafts, accessibility versions.
The voice test. After working with AI, read your piece aloud or view it alongside your earlier work. Does it sound like you? Would readers who know your work recognise it? If AI phrasing, imagery or rhythm has replaced your own, revise until your voice returns. Generic AI style — predictable metaphors, balanced triplets, smooth but empty phrases — is easy to spot and erodes distinctiveness.

Protecting craft and growth

Creative skill develops through struggle: drafting badly, revising, finding solutions. Outsourcing that struggle can stunt growth, especially for emerging writers and artists. A useful practice: write or draft first yourself, then use AI for critique or alternatives — rather than starting from AI output. Keep notebooks and drafts that show your process.

Honesty and disclosure

Audiences, publishers, competitions and grant bodies increasingly have policies on AI use. Some prohibit AI-generated content; others require disclosure; some magazines have closed submissions after floods of AI-generated stories. Read submission guidelines and disclose accurately. Presenting AI-generated work as entirely your own where that matters to others is a form of deception.

Respecting other artists

Prompting AI to imitate a living artist's distinctive style or to produce work "in the style of" a named illustrator raises ethical concerns and, in some contexts, legal ones. Many artists object to their work being used to train models without consent or compensation. Consider credit, consent and the effect of your practice on fellow artists' livelihoods.

African and diaspora creativity

AI tools trained predominantly on Western data may default to Western aesthetics, names, settings and narrative structures. African and diaspora artists can push against these defaults, insist on cultural specificity, and use their own archives, languages and forms. Your perspective is precisely what generic systems lack.

Documenting your process

Keep records of how you used AI — prompts, outputs, and how you transformed them. This supports honest disclosure, potential copyright claims based on human contribution, and your own reflection on what helped and what did not.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my creative critic, not my ghostwriter. I will paste a draft I wrote myself. Give me specific feedback on voice, imagery, pacing and structure, point out any passages that sound generic, and ask me three questions that push the piece deeper. Do not rewrite the piece; suggest at most two alternative lines as examples of a direction, which I will rework in my own words.

📚 Glossary

  • Voice: an artist's distinctive style and perspective
  • Constraint: a rule or limit used to stimulate creativity
  • Disclosure: stating how AI was used in creating work
  • Style imitation: producing work mimicking a specific artist's distinctive style

📖 References

  • Clarkesworld Magazine (2023) — statement on closing submissions due to AI-generated stories.
  • Society of Authors / Authors Guild — guidance on AI and authors.
  • Chiang, T. (2023). Will A.I. become the new McKinsey? / ChatGPT is a blurry JPEG of the web. The New Yorker.

quiz.q: A poet in Bamenda publishes a collection drafted largely by AI. Critics praise its polish, but longtime readers say it no longer sounds like her. What does the module's voice test suggest?
opts: Keep it, since critical praise shows the AI improved her craft
Revise until her own phrasing, imagery and rhythm return
Ask the AI to rewrite it in the style of her earlier books
Disclose AI use, which resolves the concern about her voice
quiz.x: The voice test asks whether readers who know her work recognise it; if not, revise until her voice returns. Disclosure (runner-up) is honest but does not restore the voice.

quiz.q: An emerging short-story writer in Accra wants AI help without stunting her development. Which workflow best protects her growth?
opts: Start from an AI draft, then rewrite each paragraph in her own words
Alternate stories, writing one alone and the next with AI
Draft first herself, then ask AI for critique or alternatives
Use AI for full drafts now, and switch to her own drafting later
quiz.x: Skill develops through struggle; drafting first then using AI for critique keeps that struggle. Rewriting an AI draft (runner-up) still starts from AI output, the practice the module advises against.

quiz.q: A writer enters a US literary competition requiring disclosure of AI use. She used AI for brainstorming titles and line edits, but wrote the story herself. What should she do?
opts: Disclose accurately how AI was used, as the rules require
Withdraw the entry, since any AI use disqualifies the work
Disclose just the line edits, since title ideas are minor
Disclose nothing, since the story itself was written by her
quiz.x: Read guidelines and disclose accurately; presenting work as fully your own where it matters is deception. Partial disclosure (runner-up) omits a use the rules require her to report.

quiz.q: An agency asks an AI model for book-cover illustrations 'in the exact style' of a named living Nigerian illustrator. What concern does the module raise?
opts: It produces lower-quality images than a generic house style would
It raises ethical and possibly legal concerns about consent and credit
It mainly risks confusing readers about which publisher released it
It is acceptable if the agency credits the illustrator on the cover
quiz.x: Imitating a living artist's distinctive style raises ethical and in some contexts legal concerns about consent, credit and livelihood. Crediting (runner-up) addresses credit but not consent or compensation.

quiz.q: An editor in Lagos reviews a manuscript and suspects heavy AI involvement. Which features most signal generic AI style?
opts: Regional idioms, Pidgin dialogue and unusual sentence lengths
Dense footnotes, archaic spellings and quoted proverbs
Predictable metaphors, balanced triplets and smooth empty phrases
Long digressions, unresolved endings and abrupt shifts in narrative tone
quiz.x: The module lists predictable metaphors, balanced triplets and smooth but empty phrases. Abrupt shifts (runner-up) can indicate weak editing but are not the distinctive AI signature.

quiz.q: A Cameroonian novelist finds AI suggestions keep defaulting to names like 'Emily' and settings like London. What does the module recommend?
opts: Accept the defaults to make the novel easier for global markets
Avoid using AI for any part of a novel set in Africa
Switch to a different AI model until the Western defaults disappear
Insist on cultural specificity, drawing on her own archives and forms
quiz.x: AI trained on Western data defaults to Western aesthetics; African artists can push back and use their own archives, languages and forms. Switching models (runner-up) may help a little but the data bias persists.

quiz.q: A visual artist in Atlanta used AI images as material and then heavily reworked them. Why should she keep records of prompts, outputs and transformations?
opts: To let the AI company verify she complied with its terms of service rules
To prove to buyers that AI did most of the technical work
To support honest disclosure and copyright claims on her human input
To train her own model later using the stored prompt history
quiz.x: Documentation supports disclosure, potential copyright claims based on human contribution, and reflection. Terms-of-service compliance (runner-up) is plausible but not the purpose the module gives.

quiz.q: A Yaounde poetry teacher asks AI to generate unusual formal rules, such as 'every line must contain a market sound', to push students out of habits. Which collaboration mode is this?
opts: Constraint generator
Critic and editor
Production support
Brainstorming partner
quiz.x: A constraint generator supplies prompts, forms or rules that push creators out of habits. Brainstorming (runner-up) generates many options to select from, rather than rules to write within.

quiz.q: In 2023 the science-fiction magazine Clarkesworld temporarily closed submissions. A Kenyan writer asks why. What is the correct explanation?
opts: Its funding ended after AI cut its advertising revenue
It was flooded with AI-generated story submissions
A court ordered it to stop accepting stories after a lawsuit
Its editors decided to publish AI-generated fiction exclusively
quiz.x: Clarkesworld closed submissions after a flood of AI-generated stories. The lawsuit option (runner-up) reflects real AI legal disputes, but none caused this closure.

quiz.q: A historical novelist in Kano uses AI to get background on 1900s trans-Saharan trade routes for her setting. How should she treat this research?
opts: Ask the AI for sources and cite them in the novel's afterword
Use it as is, since fiction does not require factual accuracy
Use it but add an author's note saying details may be wrong
Verify it independently against reliable historical sources
quiz.x: In the research-assistant mode, background must be verified independently. Asking AI for sources (runner-up) risks fabricated references, which the course warns about.

facts.t: Clarkesworld magazine closed submissions after a flood of AI-generated stories.
facts.more: Venues now set explicit AI policies — some prohibit AI content, others require disclosure. Read guidelines before submitting.

facts.t: Brainstorm, critic, research assistant, constraint generator, material, production support.
facts.more: Naming your mode keeps you in control of how much the AI contributes.

facts.more: Predictable metaphors, balanced triplets and smooth but empty phrases signal generic AI style.

modules.d: Copyright, training data, academic integrity and what originality means now.
modules.body:
Old questions, new urgency

What makes someone an author? What counts as original? Who owns a creative work? Humanists have debated these questions for centuries — from medieval scribes and collaborative workshops to Barthes's "death of the author" and the remix culture of the internet. Generative AI gives them new urgency and legal consequences.

Copyright and human authorship

In many legal systems, copyright protects works of human authorship. In the United States, the Copyright Office has refused registration for material generated by AI without sufficient human creative control, and in Thaler v. Perlmutter the federal appeals court in Washington, D.C. affirmed in 2025 that a work created autonomously by an AI system cannot be registered because human authorship is required. Human selection, arrangement and modification of AI material can be protected. Other countries take different approaches, and law is evolving — creators should check their jurisdiction.

Training data and fair use debates

AI systems are trained on vast collections of books, articles, images and music, often without explicit permission from creators. Authors, news organisations, artists and record labels have brought lawsuits in several countries — for example authors' and news publishers' cases against AI companies in the United States. Early court rulings have been mixed and many cases remain ongoing; some disputes have moved toward licensing agreements. The debate involves copyright, fair use or fair dealing, compensation and consent, and the future economics of creative work.

Academic integrity. Universities, journals and publishers have issued AI policies. Publication ethics bodies such as COPE state that AI tools cannot be listed as authors because they cannot take responsibility for the work; authors must disclose AI use and remain accountable for accuracy. Style guides such as MLA and APA provide formats for citing AI-generated content. Always follow your institution's and venue's specific rules.

What is originality now?

Originality has never meant creation from nothing; all work draws on tradition. In an AI age, originality increasingly lies in judgement (what to ask, select and reject), perspective (lived experience and situated knowledge), argument (new interpretations supported by evidence), form (distinctive structures and styles), and access (sources, communities and experiences others cannot reach). These are human contributions that AI cannot supply by itself.

Detecting AI use — and its limits

Educators sometimes rely on AI-detection software. Research and experience show these tools produce false positives and negatives, and some studies have found they disproportionately flag non-native English writers. Detection scores should never be the sole basis for accusations. Better approaches include assessment design (process, drafts, oral defence, personal reflection), clear policies and conversation.

Teaching the humanities with AI

Humanities educators can teach students to use AI critically: comparing AI interpretations with their own, identifying fabricated sources, analysing AI bias, and reflecting on authorship. Assignments that require personal voice, local sources, archival work and in-class discussion remain meaningful and resistant to outsourcing.

Your position

Humanists will disagree about AI, and that diversity is healthy. What matters is that positions are informed, transparent and consistent with professional ethics: honesty about how work is produced, respect for other creators, and accountability for what we publish.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my debate partner on AI and authorship. Present the strongest arguments on both sides of three questions: (1) Should AI-generated works receive copyright? (2) Is training AI on copyrighted works without permission fair? (3) Should students be allowed to use AI in humanities essays? Then help me draft a short, reasoned position statement for my discipline, noting where law varies by jurisdiction.

📚 Glossary

  • Human authorship: human creative contribution required for copyright in many jurisdictions
  • Fair use / fair dealing: legal doctrines allowing limited use of copyrighted material
  • COPE: Committee on Publication Ethics
  • False positive: incorrectly flagging human work as AI-generated
  • Originality: distinctive contribution of judgement, perspective, argument or form

📖 References

  • Thaler v. Perlmutter, U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit (2025).
  • U.S. Copyright Office (2025). Copyright and Artificial Intelligence, Part 2: Copyrightability.
  • COPE (2023). Authorship and AI tools — position statement.
  • Liang, W. et al. (2023). GPT detectors are biased against non-native English writers. Patterns.
  • MLA and APA style guidance on citing generative AI.

quiz.q: A US artist applies to register a work that an AI system created autonomously, listing the AI as author. Following Thaler v. Perlmutter (2025), what outcome is most likely?
opts: Registration granted, provided the artist discloses the AI system used
Registration granted, with the AI listed as author and the artist as owner
Registration deferred until Congress passes a specific AI statute
Registration refused, since human authorship is required
quiz.x: The D.C. Circuit affirmed that a work created autonomously by AI cannot be registered because human authorship is required. Disclosure (runner-up) matters for mixed works but cannot supply missing human authorship.

quiz.q: A researcher in Nairobi wants to list ChatGPT as a co-author on a journal article. Under COPE's position, why is this not acceptable?
opts: Because AI contributions are too minor to merit authorship
Because the AI tool cannot take responsibility for the work
Because the journal cannot verify the AI's institutional affiliation
Because AI companies do not consent to authorship credit
quiz.x: COPE states AI tools cannot be authors because they cannot take responsibility; humans must disclose and remain accountable. 'Too minor' (runner-up) is wrong: the issue is accountability, not size of contribution.

quiz.q: A lecturer in Buea accuses a student of AI use solely because a detector scored her essay 82% AI-generated. The student is a non-native English writer. What is the best response?
opts: Treat the score as insufficient alone and discuss drafts and process with her
Rerun the essay through a second detector and accept the average of both scores
Lower the grade quietly without a formal accusation
Uphold the accusation, since 82% is well above most detectors' thresholds
quiz.x: Detectors produce false positives, some disproportionately flag non-native writers, and scores should not be the sole basis for accusations. A second detector (runner-up) shares the same weaknesses.

quiz.q: A Cameroonian publisher asks whether training AI on copyrighted books without permission is legal in the US. Which statement best reflects the current situation?
opts: Courts have settled that such training is fair use in nearly all circumstances
US law exempts training data from copyright because it is not published
Rulings have been mixed, many cases are ongoing and some moved to licensing
Courts have ruled it infringement, and all such models must be retrained
quiz.x: Early rulings have been mixed, many cases continue and some disputes moved toward licensing; the law is evolving. Claims of settled fair use (runner-up) overstate what courts have decided.

quiz.q: A Ghanaian historian asks where originality lies when AI can produce fluent text instantly. Which answer best fits the module?
opts: In avoiding any use of existing sources or traditions in the work
In judgement, perspective, argument, form and access to sources
In using the newest AI model before other scholars adopt it
In the volume of text produced within a given deadline
quiz.x: Originality lies in judgement, perspective, argument, form and access. Avoiding tradition (runner-up for purists) is wrong: originality has never meant creation from nothing.

quiz.q: A university in Douala redesigns humanities assessment. Which design is most resistant to outsourcing to AI?
opts: Process drafts, oral defence and reflection drawing on local sources
Multiple-choice exams on the set texts taken online at home
Take-home essays with stricter word limits and plagiarism checks
Essays checked by two separate AI-detection tools before any grading begins
quiz.x: Process, drafts, oral defence and work using local sources and personal voice resist outsourcing. Dual detectors (runner-up) rely on tools known to give false positives and negatives.

quiz.q: A researcher at a US university used AI to draft a literature summary that she then checked and revised for a journal article. What do professional norms require?
opts: List the AI tool as a named contributor in the acknowledgements alone
Disclose the AI use and let the tool vendor share accountability
Disclose the AI use per venue rules and remain accountable for accuracy
No disclosure, since she verified and revised every sentence
quiz.x: COPE and venue policies require disclosure while authors stay accountable for accuracy. Sharing accountability with the vendor (runner-up) contradicts the principle that only humans take responsibility.

quiz.q: Based on the Zarya of the Dawn decision and US guidance, which part of a comic created by a Cameroonian-American author is most likely protected by copyright?
opts: The Midjourney images, since the author wrote detailed prompts
The whole comic, since the author owns the AI subscription
Nothing, since any AI use voids copyright for the entire work
The author's written story and her arrangement of panels
quiz.x: The Copyright Office protected the human-written text and arrangement, not the AI-generated images. Detailed prompts (runner-up) were not treated as enough creative control over the images.

quiz.q: A writing centre in Texas reviews AI detectors. Which group did some studies find these tools disproportionately flag as AI-generated?
opts: Students writing about technical subjects
Non-native English writers
Writers who use reference managers
Native English writers with very formal styles
quiz.x: Some studies found detectors disproportionately flag non-native English writers. Formal native writers (runner-up) can also be misflagged, but the documented disparity concerns non-native writers.

quiz.q: A Cameroonian scholar publishes an edited volume using AI for translation drafts of two chapters. Which practice best aligns with professional ethics?
opts: Omit mention of AI because the chapters were post-edited
Disclose AI use privately to the publisher but not to readers
Credit the AI tool as a co-translator on the volume's title page
State how AI was used, credit contributors and own the final text
quiz.x: Professional ethics call for honesty about how work is produced, respect for creators and accountability. Crediting AI as co-translator (runner-up) conflicts with the principle that AI cannot take responsibility.

facts.t: Thaler v. Perlmutter: D.C. Circuit affirms copyright requires human authorship.
facts.more: A work created autonomously by an AI system cannot be registered; human selection, arrangement and modification can be protected.

facts.t: Statute of Anne, the first copyright statute, enacted in Britain.
facts.more: Copyright has always been a negotiated balance between creators, publishers and the public — AI reopens that bargain.

facts.t: Barthes publishes 'The Death of the Author'.
facts.more: Long before AI, humanists questioned whether meaning lives in the author's intention or the reader's interpretation.

facts.t: COPE: AI tools cannot be listed as authors.
facts.more: They cannot take responsibility for the work. Authors must disclose AI use and remain accountable for accuracy.

modules.t: Capstone: A Work of AI-Assisted Scholarship or Art
modules.d: Produce and reflect on a scholarly or creative work that uses AI critically and transparently.
modules.body:
Your capstone

Create a work of AI-assisted scholarship or art in your discipline — a research essay, archival project, translation, digital exhibition, short story collection, poetry sequence, artwork series, or teaching unit — accompanied by a critical reflection on how AI was used.

Options

  • Archival project: transcribe and analyse a small collection using HTR or OCR, with verified transcriptions and an interpretive essay.
  • Translation project: translate a text using a machine draft and post-editing, with a translator's note explaining your choices.
  • Distant and close reading: analyse a corpus computationally and interpret the patterns through close reading.
  • Creative work: produce writing or art using AI in a defined collaborative mode, documenting your process and voice.
  • Teaching unit: design lessons that teach students to use and critique AI in a humanities subject.

Requirements

  1. The work itself, of a quality appropriate to your field.
  2. Process documentation: prompts, AI outputs and your transformations or corrections, with dates.
  3. Verification record: how you checked sources, transcriptions, translations or facts.
  4. Ethics statement: consent, copyright, cultural sensitivity and privacy considerations.
  5. Disclosure statement in the form your field would expect (e.g., MLA/APA citation or a creator's note).
  6. Critical reflection (800–1,200 words): what AI contributed, what it distorted or could not do, how your voice and judgement shaped the work, and what this suggests about your discipline's future.
Assessment criteria. Quality and originality of the work; rigour of verification; ethical and cultural responsibility; transparency of process; and depth of critical reflection. A modest project done with integrity and insight is stronger than an ambitious one done carelessly.

Sharing your work

Consider sharing your capstone with your cohort, community or institution. Humanistic engagement with AI is still being defined — your work contributes to that conversation.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my capstone supervisor. I will describe my planned project in [discipline]. Help me refine its scope, choose the AI collaboration mode, design a process documentation template and a verification plan, identify ethical issues (consent, copyright, cultural sensitivity, privacy), and outline my critical reflection. Then review my draft against the five assessment criteria.

Going deeper — capstone playbook: your work of AI-assisted scholarship or art

Humanities capstones are judged on the quality of thought, not the volume of AI use. The strongest projects choose a narrow corpus or form, keep a meticulous process log, and let the critical reflection argue something specific about what AI revealed or concealed.

Step-by-step timeline.

  • Week 1 — Scope. Choose your option and a deliberately modest corpus or form (e.g., 20 letters, one short story, a 2,000-word text to translate). Clear permissions and note cultural sensitivities. Start the process log.
  • Week 2 — Produce with AI. Generate drafts, transcriptions, translations or analyses; save prompts and outputs with dates. Begin verifying against originals, dictionaries, archives or expert readers.
  • Week 3 — Transform. Revise, correct and interpret. Mark where your judgement overrode the machine and why. Draft the ethics and disclosure statements.
  • Week 4 — Reflect and present. Write the 800–1,200-word critical reflection and prepare a short presentation with before/after examples.

Deliverables checklist.

  • ☐ The finished work
  • ☐ Process log (prompts, outputs, your changes, dates)
  • ☐ Verification record
  • ☐ Ethics statement
  • ☐ Disclosure statement in your field's format
  • ☐ Critical reflection (800–1,200 words)

Assessment rubric (weighted).

  • Quality and originality of the work — 30%: meets the standards of the discipline
  • Rigour of verification — 20%: errors caught, sources checked
  • Ethical and cultural responsibility — 15%: consent, copyright, sensitivity
  • Transparency of process — 15%: a reader could reconstruct how AI was used
  • Depth of critical reflection — 20%: specific, argued insight, not generic praise or alarm
Worked mini-example. A student translates a short Pidgin English folktale recorded in the North-West Region into standard English and French. The machine draft flattens proverbs and misreads idioms; the student consults two elder speakers, restores the proverbs with explanatory notes and documents twelve significant corrections. The reflection argues that the machine treated Pidgin as "broken English", and that this exposes a bias in what counts as a language in training data — a claim supported with concrete examples from the log.

Common failure modes.

  • Choosing a project too large to verify properly.
  • A reflection that summarises tools instead of making an argument.
  • Missing permissions for archival images, recordings or living authors' work.
  • Hiding errors instead of analysing them — errors are often the most valuable evidence.
  • Inconsistent disclosure that does not match field conventions.

Submission and presentation structure.

  • 1. The work and its question (what you set out to make or discover)
  • 2. Method: how AI was used, with one before/after example
  • 3. Verification and ethics
  • 4. Key insight from the critical reflection
  • 5. Implications for your discipline
🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as a demanding peer reviewer in my discipline [name it]. Here is my process log excerpt and draft reflection: [paste]. Identify claims in my reflection that are not supported by evidence in the log, point out where I describe tools rather than argue, and suggest two examples from my own corrections that would make my argument sharper. Do not rewrite my text; ask questions instead.

📚 Glossary

  • Process documentation: record of prompts, outputs and transformations
  • Verification record: evidence of checks on sources and outputs
  • Ethics statement: account of consent, rights and sensitivity considerations
  • Critical reflection: analysis of what AI contributed and distorted

📖 References

  • MLA Style Center — citing generative AI.
  • APA Style — how to cite ChatGPT and other AI tools.
  • Oral History Association — Principles and Best Practices.
  • Transkribus and Zotero documentation.

quiz.q: A capstone student transcribed 40 mission letters with HTR. Which required component shows readers how she checked the transcriptions against the originals?
opts: The process documentation of her prompts and outputs
The critical reflection on what AI contributed
The verification record of checks on outputs
The ethics statement on consent and privacy
quiz.x: The verification record documents how sources, transcriptions or facts were checked. Process documentation (runner-up) records prompts and outputs but not the checks themselves.

quiz.q: One student submits an ambitious 60-page digital exhibition with unverified AI citations; another a modest 15-page archival study fully verified. Under the assessment criteria, which is stronger?
opts: The archival study, since rigour and integrity outweigh scale
The exhibition, since ambition and scope earn the most credit
The exhibition, if its citations are fixed before the final grade
Both equal, since each meets the minimum length requirement
quiz.x: The module states a modest project done with integrity is stronger than an ambitious one done carelessly. Fixing citations later (runner-up) does not change that the submitted work lacked rigour.

quiz.q: A student's capstone uses photographs of a Bafut shrine and interviews with elders. Which component should address consent and cultural sensitivity?
opts: The disclosure statement
The ethics statement
The verification record
The process documentation
quiz.x: The ethics statement covers consent, copyright, cultural sensitivity and privacy. The disclosure statement (runner-up) states how AI was used, not the ethical considerations.

quiz.q: A capstone student in Lagos writes a 1,000-word reflection. Which content best meets the requirements?
opts: What AI added and distorted, and how her judgement shaped the work
A review of the AI tools she compared, ranked by their output quality
A step-by-step list of each prompt she used and its timestamp
A summary of her project's findings for a general audience
quiz.x: The reflection should cover what AI contributed, distorted or could not do, how her voice shaped the work and implications for the discipline. A prompt list (runner-up) belongs in process documentation.

quiz.q: A student wants to analyse word patterns across 500 colonial newspapers and then interpret key passages. Which capstone option fits best?
opts: Archival HTR project
Teaching unit design plan
Distant + close reading
Translation project
quiz.x: Distant and close reading combines computational analysis of a corpus with interpretation. The archival project (runner-up) focuses on transcribing and analysing a small collection.

quiz.q: A supervisor asks why the process documentation must include dated prompts and AI outputs. Which reason is most important?
opts: It allows the student to reuse the prompts in future projects
It lets the supervisor rerun the prompts later to grade the AI's own work
It meets a copyright requirement that applies to all student work
It makes the AI's and student's contributions transparent and checkable
quiz.x: Dated prompts and outputs make process transparent, supporting the transparency criterion and honest disclosure. Rerunning prompts (runner-up) would not reproduce outputs reliably and is not the purpose.

quiz.q: A student translating a Mongo Beti short story into English uses an MT draft and post-editing. Which additional element should the translation capstone include?
opts: A back-translation of the final text into French
A ranking of the MT systems she tested
A translator's note explaining her choices
A glossary generated by the AI system
quiz.x: The translation option requires a translator's note explaining choices. Back-translation (runner-up) can be a check, but the note is the specified element.

quiz.q: A capstone examiner checks whether a student was open about how the work was produced. Which assessment criterion is this?
opts: Rigour of verification
Transparency of process
Ethical and cultural responsibility
Quality and originality of the work
quiz.x: Transparency of process concerns openness about production. Rigour of verification (runner-up) concerns how facts and outputs were checked, not openness.

quiz.q: A poet in Accra uses AI only to comment on drafts she wrote herself. Which collaboration mode is she using, and what must her capstone document?
opts: Material mode, with the AI outputs she incorporated directly
Brainstorming mode, with a full list of the options the AI generated
Production support mode, with the formatting steps it handled
Critic and editor mode, with process records and her revisions
quiz.x: Using AI for feedback is the critic and editor mode, and she must document prompts, outputs and her transformations. Brainstorming (runner-up) generates possibilities rather than critiquing her drafts.

quiz.q: A Cameroonian lecturer explains the capstone's overall aim to a new cohort. Which description is most accurate?
opts: To produce AI-assisted work with critical reflection on how AI was used
To publish a work in a peer-reviewed venue before graduation
To show mastery of as many AI tools as possible within a single project
To prove that human-made work is superior to AI-assisted work
quiz.x: The capstone asks for AI-assisted scholarship or art accompanied by critical reflection. Mastering many tools (runner-up) misses that judgement and reflection matter more than tool count.

labs.title: Plan an archival capstone
labs.intro: Order the work for a small HTR/OCR archival project.
steps: Verify transcriptions and record the checks
Write the ethics and disclosure statements
labs.tip: Permissions → transcription → verification → interpretation → statements → reflection.

labs.title: Review this draft capstone reflection
labs.intro: A classmate shares part of their reflection. Tap the weaknesses a supervisor would flag.
segments: I used a machine draft for my translation of three Ewondo folktales,
then post-edited it with my grandmother, a fluent speaker.
The AI handled the proverbs perfectly, so I did not check them.
Proverbs are exactly where MT fails; unverified claims undermine the verification record.
I logged every prompt and output with dates.
I did not ask the storytellers' families, since the tales are public anyway.
Ignores consent and cultural sensitivity — an ethics statement gap.
AI did all the creative choices, which proves human translators are obsolete.
Overclaims and contradicts the human post-editing described; uncritical reflection.
The process showed me how much meaning lives in rhythm and address forms.
labs.tip: Reflection is critical when it names what AI distorted and how you checked.

plaibox.title: Capstone supervisor prompt
plaibox.intro: Describe your project and get an AI 'supervisor' to stress-test it. Your human mentor still assesses it.

fields.label: How you will verify
fields.ph: e.g. 10% sample of transcriptions checked against originals

plaibox.tip: Bring the AI's critique to your mentor — they decide.
